headline: mixed
texts: Some of the burns core is solid and some is not yet. That is normal for a topic with this many numbers and look-alike facts. The objectives below show where your answers held and where they slipped. Start with the ones marked as gaps or shaky, and use the review cards in the order listed.

Airway-first is partly there. Hold two rules together: ABCDE comes before any burn arithmetic, and swelling peaks after fluids start, so signs like hoarseness or soot mean intubate early. Revisit the airway card.

The test ladder is shaky. Keep what each test answers: bronchoscopy shows the airway, X-ray is often normal early, and oximetry cannot see carboxyhaemoglobin, so co-oximetry is needed. Redo the inhalation card.

Antidote pairing is shaky. Tie each poison to its mechanism: carbon monoxide displaces oxygen on haemoglobin, cyanide blocks cellular respiration, and unexplained lactic acidosis in smoke points to cyanide. Revisit the card.

Shock and fluid choice are shaky. Anchor on plasma loss: rising haematocrit and low urine mean hypovolaemic shock, treated with titrated Ringer lactate, and no colloid in the first 24 h of classic Parkland. Revisit the card.

Depth grading is shaky. Pain does not fall in a straight line with depth. Deep partial is mottled and less painful with sluggish refill; full thickness is leathery, non-blanching and insensate. Redo the depth card.
TBSA estimation is shaky. Re-derive the adult total (9, 9, 9, 18, 18, 18, 18, 1 makes 100) and ask age first, because infant head and leg figures are 18 and 14. Redo the TBSA card.

Parkland arithmetic is shaky. Run it in order: find time of burn, set the first half over 8 h from then, subtract fluid already given, divide by the time left. Note the exam key is 4 mL, while current practice starts near 2 mL. Redo the Parkland card.

Titration is shaky. Keep the direction and the target in mind: low urine means raise the rate by about 20-25%, high urine means lower it, and the target changes for children and electrical injury. Redo the titration card.

Topical agent pairing is shaky. Rebuild a four-row table: mafenide penetrates eschar and causes acidosis, silver sulfadiazine is painless with transient leucopenia, silver nitrate stains and lowers sodium. Redo the topical card.
Curling and Marjolin are shaky. Sort them by site and timing, not by the shared word burn: Curling is gut, early, stress ulcer; Marjolin is scar, late, squamous cell carcinoma. Redo the ulcer card.
Escharotomy is shaky. Both qualifiers must hold: full-thickness eschar that is inelastic, and circumferential constriction with falling pulses or restricted chest movement. Redo the escharotomy card.
You changed your mind once you saw the qualifier. The 4 mL reflex can return under exam pressure, so read the stem for words like current or modified before you compute.
You moved the clock to the time of burn. Under pressure, now feels like time zero, so check the burn time first.
You corrected where the half goes. Under pressure the phrase half in 8 hours can slip onto the wrong quantity, so rebuild it: total, half, divide by hours.
You started deducting pre-hospital fluid. Under pressure the formula number feels complete, so ask what has already been given.
You switched to child figures after the slip. The adult chart is a strong default under pressure, so ask age first.
You separated Parkland from the colloid formulae. Under pressure Evans, Brooke and Parkland blur, so recall the pairs before choosing.
You moved from the familiar test to the confirming one. Under pressure a normal X-ray tempts reassurance, so keep the ladder in mind.
You learned why oximetry misleads. It is a favoured exam trap and a normal number is reassuring under pressure, so ask whether carbon monoxide is possible first.
You sorted the two ulcers after a swap. Both say burn, so pair each with its organ and timing again when you are rushed.
You moved from delivering the formula to titrating it. Under pressure the first calculated number feels like the order, so check urine output hourly.
You reversed your direction after the slip. Under pressure high output can feel like a signal for more fluid, so ask what it says about perfusion.
You learned to use blanching and sensation, not pain alone. Under pressure less painful can still pull you towards full thickness.
You linked the target to child and electrical settings. Under pressure the adult figure is the first one retrieved, so check age and injury type.
You fixed the swapped figures. Under pressure 9 and 18 get transposed, so recheck the total of 100.
You added both escharotomy qualifiers after the slip. Under pressure deep reads as cut, so ask about full thickness and compromise.
You corrected the agent pairs. Under pressure silver sulfadiazine becomes the default, so recall each agent's own property.
You separated the two poisons. Under pressure one fire means one oxygen treatment, so name each by mechanism.
You reordered the plan to put the airway first. Under pressure the burn-specific calculation feels like the real work, so run ABCDE first.
You changed to acting before the oedema. A comfortable patient is the temptation under pressure, so react to soot and hoarseness, not to current comfort.
You moved to plasma loss as the cause. Under pressure septic or cardiogenic look-alikes pull, so start from the rising haematocrit.
You tend to get the order or the clock wrong: arrival for burn time, calculation for airway, waiting for action. Write the steps in sequence and ask what first, and why.
You tend to mix up figures that you hold as a list: halves, rates, urine targets and region values. Anchor each number to the quantity it describes, and check totals such as 100 for TBSA.

You tend to apply a default rule across patients without checking the qualifier: adult chart for children, deep burn for escharotomy. Make the qualifier your first check: age, thickness, constriction.

You tend to swap pairs held as separate facts: formulae and fluids, agents and side effects, antidotes and poisons, eponyms. Use a small table or a one-line contrast for each set rather than recalling items alone.
You tend to stop at the familiar test and trust it, such as X-ray or oximetry. Ask what each test actually measures before you let it reassure you.

You tend to name a condition from its most visible feature rather than its cause or discriminator, in depth grading and shock type. Before answering, ask what separates this from its look-alike: blanching and sensation for depth, haematocrit and plasma loss for shock.

Twice or more you tapped Sure on an answer that was wrong. Those confident errors are the ones to fix first, so their cards are listed first. Before tapping Sure, name the qualifier in the stem that makes you certain.
You did not ask for hints, so each slip was an unaided attempt. Next time, when two options feel close, open a hint before committing. It is cheaper to ask than to rehearse the wrong model.

Work the review cards in the order shown: confident errors first, then gaps, then shaky objectives. Do one card per objective, say the answer aloud, then check. Rerun the module after a day and aim to change your first answers, not only your retries.
